profile.summary: PiFold designs an amino acid sequence for a protein backbone you supply: the inverse of structure prediction. It represents the backbone as a graph of residues, with features built by its own residue featurizer, and predicts all residues in one pass instead of one at a time. The authors report 51.66% sequence recovery on CATH 4.2 with inference about 70 times faster than autoregressive methods.

summary_quotes.text: The inputs are protein structures, and outputs are protein sequences expected to fold into the input structures.
we propose PiFold, which contains a novel residue featurizer and PiGNN layers to generate protein sequences in a one-shot way with improved recovery
PiFold could achieve 51.66\% recovery on CATH 4.2, while the inference speed is 70 times faster than the autoregressive competitors

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The backbone is turned into a graph: each residue is a node, joined to its 30 nearest neighbours. A residue featurizer builds the node and edge features, including learnable virtual atoms meant to carry information that the real atom positions do not. Ten PiGNN layers then pass messages, mixing node, edge and global context. The decoder emits every residue at once, which is what makes it faster than autoregressive inverse folding models, and training optimises perplexity against the native sequence.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: There is one method and one release. The Training&Data release, published 2023-03-05, carries a trained checkpoint.pth plus the cath4.2 and ts datasets, but the README does not document how to load it, so a PiFold result usually depends on a model someone trained or on the Colab notebooks. The code calls the method ProDesign, its earlier name, and main.py trains from scratch on CATH or TS50 with the defaults in parser.py (batch size 8, learning rate 0.001, up to 100 epochs, seed 111) before testing. A result should say which dataset split, which seed and which checkpoint or notebook it came from.

facts.label: Model type
facts.value: Inverse folding (structure-based protein design): it predicts an amino acid sequence for a given protein backbone, in one pass rather than residue by residue.

quotes.text: The inputs are protein structures, and outputs are protein sequences expected to fold into the input structures.
generate protein sequences in a one-shot way with improved recovery

facts.label: Architecture
facts.value: A residue featurizer plus stacked PiGNN graph layers. The featurizer builds node and edge features and adds learnable virtual atoms; the PiGNN mixes information at node, edge and global context level. Defaults in parser.py: 10 encoder layers, hidden, node and edge dimensions 128, 30 neighbours per residue, 3 virtual atoms.

quotes.text: the residue featurizer constructs comprehensive residue features and creates learnable virtual atoms to capture information complementary to real atoms

The PiGNN 
considers multi-scale residue interactions in node, edge, and global context levels.

facts.label: Inputs
facts.value: A protein backbone structure. The code reads the CATH or TS50 datasets through its own loaders; the repository also has an example directory, whose contents the sources read do not list.
facts.source_locator: ReadMe.md: Framework; parser.py CATH dataset parameters; repository root listing

facts.label: Outputs
facts.value: A designed amino acid sequence per backbone. The code reports perplexity and recovery (the fraction of residues matching the native sequence), overall and per CATH category.

quotes.text: outputs are protein sequences expected to fold into the input structures

facts.label: Parameters

no_run_guide_reason: The repository gives no installation steps, no dependency list and no inference script. A trained checkpoint.pth is published as a release asset, but nothing in the sources read says how to load it or run a design. main.py trains a model from scratch on CATH or TS50 and expects the dataset under ./data/, which the sources do not say how to arrange. The README's only usage route is two Google Colab notebooks, which were not opened.
notes: A trained checkpoint is published as a GitHub release asset (Training&Data, 2023-03-05); the README never mentions it, and nothing documents how to load it, so weights_licence is the repository's MIT taken to cover the asset and gated is null rather than false. released is the date the host records for the weights, the same rule used for the other models in this batch. The repository's README file is named ReadMe.md, not README.md. The code names the method ProDesign throughout, its earlier name. The record's existing source is a benchmark paper on protein-protein interaction prediction, which may have used PiFold embeddings from its own trained model; nothing here describes that use. The authors direct new users to knowledge-design in A4Bio/OpenCPD, which would be a separate record.
